habit_line: Focus habit: Wonder - Invite a question or a what-if before any answer is given. Say: “What could we ask? What if we changed one thing?” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: Welcome, Digit Detectives! Every 3-digit number is made of just three digits, but WHERE a digit sits changes everything.
Today we find every number hiding in a set of digit cards, and we make sure we do not miss any. Notice it. Test it. Explain why.
do: Focus habit: Wonder - Invite a question or a what-if before any answer is given. Say: “What could we ask? What if we changed one thing?” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: Draw three boxes on your whiteboard: hundreds, tens, ones. I will turn over one digit card at a time. As soon as you see it, write it in a box. No moving it later!
Try to make the BIGGEST number. Where will you put a 9? Where will you put a 1? Why?
You have the cards 3, 5 and 8. How many different 3-digit numbers do you think you can make with them? Write your guess in the corner of your whiteboard.
stuck: Stuck: put the 3 in the hundreds place first. What can the other two cards do?
Not sure if you have them all: “How many numbers start with 3? With 5? With 8?”
Finished early: add a 0 card and make numbers with 0, 3 and 5. Why are there fewer?

say: “5 hundreds, 12 tens and 4 ones. 12 tens is 120, so the number is 500 + 120 + 4 = 624. I can also see it as 6 hundreds, 2 tens, 4 ones, because 10 of the tens make another hundred.”

“Cards 1, 6 and 9. I keep the hundreds digit the same and swap the other two. 1 first: 169, 196. 6 first: 619, 691. 9 first: 916, 961. Each card starts 2 numbers, and 3 cards make 6 numbers. That is how I know I have them all.”

“The biggest number has the biggest digit in the hundreds place: 961. The smallest has the smallest digit in the hundreds place: 169. But zero can never go first: 036 would be just 36 (thirty-six), which has only 2 digits, so it is not a 3-digit number.”

do: Ask: “How many of your numbers start with this card? Is that all of them?”
Ask: “What is this digit worth? How many tens is that?”
Ask: “Point to the number one square below this one on the chart. How much bigger is it?”
stuck: Hint 2: “Build it with blocks: hundreds, tens and ones. Can 10 tens become a hundred?”
Hint 3: “Say the numbers out loud as you count on in 10s. What happens after 590?”

do: Ask: “How many of your numbers start with this card? Is that all of them?”
Ask: “What is this digit worth? How many tens is that?”
Ask: “Point to the number one square below this one on the chart. How much bigger is it?”
stuck: Hint 2: “Build it with blocks: hundreds, tens and ones. Can 10 tens become a hundred?”
Hint 3: “Say the numbers out loud as you count on in 10s. What happens after 590?”

say: “Which is bigger, 401 or 399? Ali says 399 because it has two 9s. Who agrees?”
ask: “Which is bigger, 401 or 399? Ali says 399 because it has two 9s. Who agrees?”
401 is bigger. Compare the hundreds first: 4 hundreds is more than 3 hundreds, so the tens and ones do not matter. Count on from 399: 400, 401.

say: “You were real detectives today: you made a list in order, so no number could hide from you.”
“Hand me your exit ticket and I will stamp your inquiry journal.”

p2l1-title.note: Objective: Read and build 3-digit numbers by place value (also with more than 9 tens), make every number from a set of digit cards by listing in order, find the biggest and smallest, and use patterns on a 1000 chart to count on and back in 1s, 10s and 100s. Thinking strategies taught today: MAKE A LIST IN ORDER and LOOK FOR A PATTERN. Materials: Digit cards 0 to 9 (one set per child), place-value mat (hundreds, tens, ones), base-ten blocks or paper strips and squares, mini whiteboards, the 1000-chart pieces on the workbook page (rows of 10). Online: children cut out paper digit cards before the lesson and move them on camera; the tutor writes on the 1000-chart pieces on the slides. Time plan: opening 0 to 1.5, sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 6, warm-up 6 to 10.5, explore 10.5 to 23.5, mini-lesson 23.5 to 35.5, brain break 35.5 to 38.5, worksheet page 1 38.5 to 52.5, check together, page 1 52.5 to 55, short teaching 55 to 59.5, worksheet page 2 59.5 to 71, check together, page 2 71 to 73.5, flex (spare time) 73.5 to 76.5, talk time 76.5 to 81.5, exit ticket 81.5 to 86.5, looking back 86.5 to 88.5, closing and stamps 88.5 to 90. The Think harder and Go further slides are optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Kit ready at minute 0: ask families to put every item on the desk before the lesson starts (a 30-second check at the start). SPINE: Today's tool is List every way. Write each way down, in order, so none is missed. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook. HABIT: Focus habit: Wonder. Invite a question or a what-if before any answer is given. Say: "What could we ask? What if we changed one thing?" Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

p2l1-tool.note: SPINE: Show for about 20 seconds, inside the opening. Today's tool is List every way. Write each way down, in order, so none is missed. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook. Eight tools: see your Toolbox Card.

p2l1-precheck.note: Minutes 1.5 to 6. Sneak-peek puzzles: two puzzles on the key idea of today, which the children have NOT learnt yet. Say out loud (about 28 words): "Two sneak-peek puzzles on ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome, so is I do not know. Nobody is marked. Say your answer together on three." Question 1 is an access question: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win (about 45 seconds). Question 2 is the thinking question (about 90 seconds). Then about 2 minutes for the answers slide and the move on. Answers are PRIVATE: each child writes on their own paper and says the answer together on three; nothing is held up to the camera. Do not raise whiteboards together, do not read answers out, do not name children. Q1 answer: 325. Listen for: Hundreds first, then tens, then ones. A drawing of 3 flats, 2 rods and 5 units is welcome. This is a first win for everyone. Q2 answer: 4 numbers: 407, 470, 704, 740. Listen for: 0 cannot be the hundreds digit, so only 4 and 7 can start. Listing in order: 4 starts 2 numbers, 7 starts 2 numbers. A child who says 6 is using 3 x 2 x 1 without the zero rule: a good idea, not a mistake to correct yet. At the end click to show the answers as "one way to think about it", without saying who had what. Ask only for volunteers: "Would anyone like to tell us how they started?" Invite the WHOLE group at once, never one child: "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Never announce who is on which page. Pairs are not split unless both children agree. Children can move either way at any time. Everyone joins explore, the mini-lesson, the check-together slides and talk time.

p2l1-warm1.note: Minutes 6 to 8.5. Place It Right. Children draw three boxes on a whiteboard: H, T, O. Shuffle digit cards 0 to 9 and turn over one at a time (online: read the digit aloud; nothing is held up to the camera). After EACH card, children write it in one empty box at once and cannot move it. After three cards, read the numbers aloud: biggest wins. Play 2 rounds (about 2.5 minutes): one for the biggest, one for the smallest. Click to show the thinking question. Talk: "A 9 goes in the hundreds: it is worth 900 there. A 0 goes in the ones. A 5 is tricky: are there more big cards or small cards left?" Listen for children who say "the hundreds digit matters most". That idea comes back in talk time (401 or 399). Bonus bubble (a choice for anyone who would like more): biggest 900, smallest 108 (the hundreds digit cannot be 0). A game of about 2.5 minutes: stop it on the clock even if the game is not finished.

p2l1-warm2.note: Minutes 8.5 to 10.5. Read each aloud, write it, say the answer together on three, then click to show. Ask after question 2: "Why did the hundreds digit change?" (9 tens and 1 more ten make 10 tens, which is another hundred). Answers: 462 and 306. Spare questions in the guide table: 80, 305, 999. Ask quick questions 1 and 3 only (about 2 minutes): children answer by thumbs, hands, not by naming a child. The other questions are spare.

p2l1-explore1.note: Minutes 10.5 to 19.5. Pairs work with digit cards 3, 5 and 8 (online: paper cards on camera). Ask them to predict first: how many numbers? Most children guess 3 or 9. Let them record numbers in any order at first; the teaching part shows how to list them in order. Any child who would like more: add a 0 card and use 0, 3, 5. Why are there fewer numbers? Go further (a second what-if, so nobody waits) is the box at the foot of this slide; the question is also posted in the chat when the pairs go to their breakout rooms. It is for ANY child who finishes the explore task or wants more: say it to the whole group as a choice, never as a prize, and never name who tries it. Pairs stay together unless both children agree to split. Answer: 24: 4 choices of which card to leave out, and each set of 3 cards makes 6 numbers (4 x 6 = 24). Take it at the debrief only if a pair offers it.

p2l1-explore2.note: Minutes 19.5 to 23.5. Let pairs keep working, then gather them. Collect the numbers on the board in the order children say them, messy on purpose, then ask "Is anything missing? Is anything there twice?" Answers: 1) 6 numbers: 358, 385, 538, 583, 835, 853. 2) List them in order: 2 numbers start with 3, 2 start with 5, 2 start with 8. 3) 853 is biggest (biggest digit in the hundreds place), 358 is smallest. Do NOT tell the method yet if nobody finds it: the next slides teach it. Keep it moving (about 4 minutes in all): ask "how do you know?" on question 2 only; about 15 seconds of talk on the other questions.

p2l1-teach1.note: Minutes 23.5 to 25.5. Teach. Build it with base-ten blocks (online: paper strips and squares). Ask first: "Can we write 5, 12, 4 as 5124?" (No: that is a 4-digit number. A box can only hold one digit.) Click through the steps. Think-aloud: "12 tens is too many for the tens box. Ten of them swap for one hundred. Now I have 6 hundreds, 2 tens and 4 ones: 624." Go the other way too: "624 is 6 hundreds and 2 tens. It is ALSO 5 hundreds and 12 tens."

p2l1-try1.note: Minutes 25.5 to 27. Write it, say the answer together on three, then click. a) Watch for 39: the 0 tens still needs a 0 to hold the place. b) 11 tens = 1 hundred and 1 ten, so 3 hundreds, 1 ten, 5 ones. (The old item c, the 6 in 461, is asked in warm-up question 2 of the guide list and dropped here.)

p2l1-we1.note: Minutes 27 to 30. Make a list in order: this is today's main strategy. Click to reveal each number while children say it first. Think-aloud: "I keep 1 in the hundreds place. The 6 and 9 can go 6, 9 or 9, 6: 169, 196. Nothing else starts with 1. Now 6 first …" Ask: "How do we KNOW there are no more?" (every card has had its turn at the front, and each one only starts 2 numbers). Then the biggest and smallest, read straight from the list.

p2l1-try2.note: Minutes 30 to 31.5. Whiteboards. The list: 348, 384, 438, 483, 834, 843. Ask a child to explain how they know there are exactly 6. Ask: "Which of the 6 is closest to 400?" (384 is only 16 away; 438 is 38 away).

p2l1-teachzero.note: Minutes 31.5 to 34.5. Teach before the worksheet (Q3 has a zero card). Ask first: "Will 0, 3, 6 make 6 numbers like before?" Let children argue. Show 036 on a calculator or say it aloud: "thirty-six". Click through. Smallest is 306, not 036. Biggest is 630. Ask a volunteer who already knows why to explain "zero can never go first" in two sentences (a job for anyone who would like it, never a named child).

p2l1-key.note: Minutes 34.5 to 35.5. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Writing 6 hundreds, 15 tens and 2 ones as 6152 instead of regrouping 15 tens as 1 hundred and 5 tens (752). (2) Listing digit-card numbers at random, so one is missed or written twice, or counting 059 as a 3-digit number. (3) Counting back in 10s across a hundred: 512, 502, 592 instead of 492.

p2l1-break.note: Minutes 35.5 to 38.5. Three minutes: two of movement, one for a drink of water. Online: each child lays out 3 digit cards in a row on camera and reads the number; call a swap and everyone shows the new number. Ask each time: bigger or smaller? Ask: "Which swap makes the biggest jump?" (swapping the hundreds digit).

p2l1-ws1.note: Minutes 38.5 to 52.5. Walk around. Ask "How do you know you have them all?" before giving any help. Q1c is the hardest on this page: 830 is 8 hundreds and 3 tens, and ALSO 7 hundreds and 13 tens (break one hundred into 10 tens). Say once, to everyone: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Never say who is on which page. Invite the WHOLE group at once, never one child: "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Pairs are not split unless both children agree.

p2l1-ws1ans.note: Minutes 52.5 to 55. Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q1b: 15 tens = 1 hundred and 5 tens, so 7 hundreds, 5 tens, 2 ones. Q2c: 472 is 28 away from 500, 427 is 73 away, 724 is 224 away. Q2d: a number is odd when its ones digit is odd; only 7 is odd, so the numbers ending in 7.

p2l1-teachchart.note: Minutes 55 to 57.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4 has chart pieces). Look for a pattern: point along a row (+1 each time) and down a column (+10 each time; the ones digit stays the same). Ask: "What is directly below 296 (one square down)? It is not on our piece!" Go down a column: 296, 306, because 10 more than 296 crosses the hundred. Directly above 281 (one square up) is 10 less: 271.

p2l1-teachriddle.note: Minutes 57.5 to 59.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q6). Two strategies together: make a list in order, then check each one (guess and check, but tidy). Ask after step 2: "Why can we stop?" (the totals go up by 2 each time, so 11 only comes once). For the "find all" line: hundreds digit 1 leaves 1 for the tens and ones (101, 110); hundreds digit 2 leaves 0 (200). Zero cannot be the hundreds digit.

p2l1-ws2.note: Minutes 59.5 to 71. Children work alone. Q4(b) and the whole of Q5 are marked ★ take-home on the page: children do them at home, so the teaching slide for Q5 (counting past a hundred) is not shown in class; its idea is on the answer slide. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson, especially children who still write 592 after 502. Tutor rule at minute 59.5: if the clock is more than 2 minutes late, drop the last Core question of page 2 to take-home (children draw a star beside it). Never shorten talk time, the exit ticket, looking back or the closing. Questions marked with a star and the words take-home on the page are done at home; their answers are still on the check-together slide.

p2l1-ws2ans.note: Minutes 71 to 73.5. Click after a child explains. Q4 Piece B: the square under 586 is 596; left 595, right 597; under 596 is 606. Q4b: 385, 395, 405. Q4(b) and Q5 are take-home stars: do not use class time on them, children self-mark at home with these answers. (Q5 trap: counting back across a hundred, 608 then 598, not 698.) Q6a: tens and ones pairs (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 4), (3, 5): only 4 + 3 + 5 = 12. Q6b: hundreds 1 leaves 2 (102, 111, 120), hundreds 2 leaves 1 (201, 210), hundreds 3 leaves 0 (300).

p2l1-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Open to any child who chooses it (the choice after question 3 on the worksheet). These are the SAME four questions as the printed Think harder page: the slide shows 1 to 3 and question 4 is on the page only. Never announce who is working on which page. Answers: 1) 4 numbers: 629, 692, 926, 962. The hundreds digit must be 6 or 9 (a number that starts with 2 is smaller than 500). With 6 in the hundreds, the other two cards make 629 and 692; with 9 in the hundreds, they make 926 and 962. 2) 3 numbers: 447, 474, 744. The two 4s look the same, so swapping them does not make a new number. 3) Ali: 46 tens is 460. Siti: 3 hundreds and 15 tens is 300 + 150 = 450. Ali has the bigger number, by 10. 4) (Question: Mei says: “If I swap the tens digit and the ones digit of a 3-digit number, the new number is always smaller.” Is she right? Show what happens with some examples. When does the number stay the same?) No. 452 becomes 425, which is smaller, but 425 becomes 452, which is bigger. It gets smaller when the tens digit is bigger than the ones digit, bigger when it is smaller, and stays the same when the two digits are the same (733).

p2l1-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. These are Think Harder Q7 and Q5. Answers: 1) 120 (100 in the hundreds place, 10 in the tens place from 330 to 339, 10 in the ones place 303, 313 … 393). 2) 381, for example 135 + 246 (1 and 2 in the hundreds, 3 and 4 in the tens, 5 and 6 in the ones).

p2l1-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Show after pairs have tried the Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What do you notice? Which place matters most in Q2? Can you count the 3s one place at a time in Q1? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p2l1-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time). Use after pairs have tried. Q1: a list in order by PLACE stops us missing any 3s; many children say 111 or 102 because they count 333 once. Q2: the hundreds digits matter most, so they get the smallest cards; any way of placing 1, 2 / 3, 4 / 5, 6 gives 381 (136 + 245 also works). Check by adding: 135 + 246 = 381.

p2l1-talk.note: Minutes 76.5 to 81.5. Pairs talk for 90 seconds, then two volunteers share. Answer: 401 is bigger. Compare the hundreds first: 4 hundreds is more than 3 hundreds, so the tens and ones do not matter. Count on from 399: 400, 401. Praise the reasons, not only the answers. Talk time rules: you choose volunteers first ("Who would like to share?"); never cold-call a child by name; any child may say pass; no public tallies, scores or rankings.

p2l1-exit.note: Minutes 81.5 to 86.5. Answer: biggest 620, smallest 206 (not 026, which is not a 3-digit number). Extension: use any three of the cards 1, 3, 5 and 7. How many different 3-digit numbers can you make? (24) Children keep slips on their desks and tick them against the answer on the next click; nothing is held up. About 2 minutes of child work.

p2l1-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 86.5 to 88.5. Start the timer (90 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. After the look-back, minutes 88.5 to 90 are flex time (the buffer): finish stamps, then goodbye. Do not start anything new. HABIT: Focus habit: Wonder. Invite a question or a what-if before any answer is given. Say: "What could we ask? What if we changed one thing?" Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.
